## Additional information for data providers [...] You should follow the 3 step method to use the index.

Defra applies the DAQI to its air quality forecasts to tell you what pollution levels are predicted to be the next day. The forecasts are provided to allow you to plan ahead and where relevant, take the recommended action to reduce the effects of air pollution. In addition, Defra's latest air pollution monitoring data are displayed using the same index and this tells you what pollution has been like.

The overall air pollution index for a site or region is determined by the highest concentration of five pollutants:

 Nitrogen Dioxide
 Sulphur Dioxide
 Ozone
 Particles < 2.5µm (PM2.5)
 Particles < 10µm (PM10)

local_documents.title: Source Sector and Fuel Contributions to Ambient PM2.5 Mortality
local_documents.snippet: Source Sector and Fuel Contributions to Ambient PM2.5 Mortality Source Sector and Fuel Contributions to Ambient PM2.5 Mortality This paper provides a global assessment of which sectors and fuels contribute most to ambient PM2.5 exposure and PM2.5-attributable mortality. The motivation is practical: fine particulate matter is the world's leading environmental health risk, but effective air quality policy requires knowing which sources drive the burden in different places. The study covers 21 world regions, 204 countries, and 200 sub-national areas, allowing comparison across global, national, and urban-relevant scales. The methodology combines atmospheric modeling, satellite-based exposure estimates, emissions inventories, and disease-specific health risk functions. local_documents.title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines
local_documents.snippet: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines The WHO global air quality guidelines provide health-based recommendations for reducing exposure to major outdoor air pollutants: PM2.5, PM10, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and carbon monoxide. The central message is that air pollution is the single largest environmental threat to human health and causes millions of deaths and lost healthy life years each year. The burden is now described as comparable to major global risks such as unhealthy diets and tobacco smoking. The guidelines update the previous WHO air quality guidance published in 2006. WHO explains that the evidence base expanded substantially over the intervening 15 years, including studies from lower-pollution high-income settings and from low- and middle-income countries experiencing rapid urbanization and industrial growth. local_documents.snippet: Clean Air Strategy 2019 Executive Summary Clean Air Strategy 2019 Executive Summary The Clean Air Strategy presents the UK government's plan to reduce air pollution from all major sources, improve public health, protect the natural environment, and support cleaner economic growth. It begins from the position that the country has already reduced many of the worst pollution problems through regulation, industrial investment, and a cleaner energy mix, but that air pollution remains one of the UK's largest public health challenges. The strategy stresses that harmful emissions now come from many diffuse sources, not only from large factories or road traffic. The document identifies air pollution as a result of how the UK generates power, heats homes, produces food, manufactures goods, and moves people and freight. local_documents.title: Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany
local_documents.snippet: Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany This study estimates the health burden in Germany caused by long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 emissions from hard coal- and lignite-fired power plants in 2015. The authors focus on source-specific disease burden rather than total air pollution, asking how much disease could be attributed specifically to emissions from these coal power plants. The central conclusion is that both hard coal and lignite contributed a measurable burden of disease, with lignite producing the larger impact for both pollutants. The methodology combines air pollution modeling, population exposure assessment, and health burden calculation. local_documents.title: Analysis and Optimal Control of a Fractional Order Influenza Epidemic Model
local_documents.snippet: Epidemic Model This paper develops a mathematical model for seasonal influenza that explicitly accounts for memory effects, meaning that current disease transmission is influenced by earlier biological and environmental conditions. The authors connect this idea to prolonged exposure to ambient air pollution, especially pollutants such as PM2.5, NO2, and SO2, which can weaken respiratory defenses and increase susceptibility over periods longer than a typical influenza infection. The central claim is that standard ordinary differential equation models can miss these lingering effects because they treat disease dynamics as depending mainly on the present state of the population. The model is a fractional-order SEImIsHRD system. It separates the population into susceptible, exposed, mildly infectious, severely infectious, hospitalized, recovered, and dead groups.
